vignette:
Omar Haddad was 40 when he came to treatment, a married software engineer who had once described himself as steady, optimistic, and easy to live with. He traced the change in himself to the day a powerful earthquake struck while he was visiting family in a densely built neighborhood. He had been inside a multistory apartment building when the shaking began, abrupt enough that at first he thought something mechanical had exploded beneath the floor. Then came the deeper roar of the building moving against itself, the crack of concrete, car alarms outside, and the screaming of people in the stairwell. Omar remembered trying to get out, but his memory of the next minutes broke apart when he tried to tell it. He would start with the lights going out, then jump to the sound of glass breaking, then to being pressed against a wall, then back again to the first violent sway. What remained clearest were not the steps in order but the sensory fragments: the grinding noise, the cries, the dust in his mouth, the feeling that the air itself had turned dangerous.

In the weeks after he returned home to the United States, Omar found that the memories did not come back as stories so much as as total experiences. A sound in his environment could suddenly bring back the roar he had heard inside the collapsing building, and for a few moments it felt to him as if he were there again all at once, hearing, sensing, and reliving the event rather than merely remembering it. When he tried to explain this to his wife, he said that it was not like “thinking about it”; it was as if his whole body got pulled back into the scene before his mind could catch up. At other times he became preoccupied with trying to reconstruct exactly what had happened, circling through details repeatedly and getting stuck on parts that would not line up. He would say that if he could only put it in the right sequence, maybe it would stop feeling so unreal and so present at the same time.

Outside the home, Omar began moving through the world as if danger could break open anywhere. In restaurants, office conference rooms, and even at his son’s school events, he checked exits before he could settle. He chose seats at the edge of the room and noticed stairwells, doors, and open pathways automatically. At work, where he spent long hours in a busy open-plan engineering office, he was especially tense. If a coworker rolled a chair suddenly behind him or stood up quickly in his peripheral vision, Omar reacted with a jolt before he knew what he was doing. If someone touched his shoulder unexpectedly to get his attention, he flinched sharply and sometimes stood up as if he needed to move away. He felt embarrassed afterward, but in the instant it happened he was certain his body was responding to immediate danger.

He also began avoiding reminders that felt too close to the bodily vulnerability of that day. He postponed routine physical exams and refused to accompany relatives to the hospital when they needed support. Even the sight of an ambulance made him turn his eyes away or change direction. He could not easily explain this except to say that anything medical now made him feel trapped and exposed, as if he were again in the aftermath of disaster waiting for bad news or injury to become undeniable.

In his own mind, Omar had grown harsh and hopeless. He had come to believe that someone stronger, more decisive, or more capable would not have ended up in that situation as he did. Although he knew an earthquake was not something a person causes, he compared himself unfavorably to an imagined other man who would have handled it better. He told himself there was no real future left for him to look forward to, that nothing good could happen anymore because the world had already shown its worst face. What troubled him almost as much was his sense of who he had become. He said he used to be a happy person, the one in the family who lightened things, and now he was miserable nearly all the time.

Omar tried to manage this by forcing himself toward positivity. When memories surfaced or his wife asked how he was doing, he pushed himself to say that he was lucky, that others had suffered more, that he needed to focus only on the bright side. The effort had a strained quality; he was not comforted by these thoughts so much as trying to shut down anything darker before it could spread. Alongside that, he spent long stretches mentally occupied with anger and fantasies of getting even with whoever had built unsafely, ignored warnings, or allowed standards to slip. He knew there was no single assailant in the usual sense, yet his mind kept returning to the idea that someone was responsible and should be made to pay.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing in daily life. At work he was distracted by where the exits were and by his own reactions to nearby movement. At home his wife experienced him as distant, brittle, and unreachable, either insisting everything was fine or disappearing into brooding silence. He finally agreed to therapy after startling violently when a colleague touched him from behind during a routine discussion, leaving him shaken and ashamed for hours. What frightened Omar most was the thought that this was permanent, that the version of himself who felt safe, hopeful, and recognizably happy was gone for good. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to feel that his life still had a future and that the memory of the earthquake could become something he remembered rather than something he kept re-entering.
